title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
hook: Martin Luther King Jr, jailed, writes to fellow clergy that injustice in one place threatens justice in every place

segments.voice: Yesterday, Billy Graham, an old hymn, and ropes coming down. Your line was just as I am. Who did you invite, and did they come? Day nine hundred sixty.

A cell in the Birmingham city jail. A pastor has been arrested for leading a march in defiance of a court order. Someone brings him a newspaper, and in it is a public statement from a group of white clergymen in the city. They call the demonstrations unwise and untimely. They say outsiders are stirring up trouble, and the right course is patience and the courts. The pastor has no desk and not much paper. The story goes that he starts writing his answer in the margins of that very newspaper, and on scraps smuggled in and out. The pastor is Martin Luther King Jr., and he is writing to fellow ministers. Today, his letter.

King wrote as a minister to ministers, and the letter is full of the Bible and the church. To the charge that he was an outsider, he answered that he was in Birmingham because injustice was there. He compared himself to the apostle Paul, who left his home town to carry the gospel to other cities. And then he made a claim readers still quote: injustice in one place is a threat to justice in every place. In his picture, all people are bound together in a single garment of destiny, so a tear in one part runs through the whole cloth. What happens to one city happens, in the end, to everyone. To the charge that the time wasn't right, he wrote that for Black Americans the word wait had nearly always meant never. And to the question of breaking laws, he reached back to Augustine and Thomas Aquinas, saints of the church, to argue that an unjust law is no true law at all, while insisting that anyone who breaks one must do it openly, lovingly, and accept the penalty. He also reached for the prophet Amos. In the King James Bible, Amos says: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." Not a trickle, saved for a better season. A river. Some of the letter's sharpest words aren't aimed at open enemies. They're aimed at the white moderate, who agrees with the goal in principle and keeps asking for patience, and at white churches that stood by. King wrote with grief about the church, not against it. He was a pastor, disappointed in his own house, and he still called it home.

Here's the practice: speak for justice somewhere. Settle, and breathe. Think of one unfairness close to you that isn't happening to you. A coworker always talked over. A neighbor without a ramp. A rule at school that lands harder on some kids than others. Don't solve it yet. Just look at it plainly, and notice the part of you that wants to say it's not the right time. Then choose one small, honest word you could say, to whom, and when. If you pray, you can hold Amos's line about justice running down like water. The bell holds the time.
Birmingham, where Martin Luther King Jr. wrote from a cell to fellow clergy who had told him to wait.
Your line: justice is all one piece. Today, say the one honest word you chose, kindly and clearly, about an unfairness that isn't yours. Day nine hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Some Christians read King's letter in churches, classrooms and study groups, and some congregations read parts of it aloud together.

attack them by name in the press.
fork.reveal: King wrote a long reply to his fellow clergy, full of scripture and church teaching, answering each charge in turn.

notes: King's letter is under copyright: every line of it is paraphrased, not quoted (injustice anywhere / network of mutuality / single garment of destiny / wait has almost always meant never / an unjust law is no law at all). Confirm the paraphrases are fair.

The margins-of-the-newspaper account is hedged as 'the story goes'; confirm.
King's use of the apostle Paul, Augustine and Aquinas, and the 'white moderate' passage; confirm summary.
